messages.subject: question regarding iid2d
messages.body_plain:
In the first example (p.3) for iid2d, it's said that we're simulating the model

    y|eta ~ Poisson

Can someone show me where the Poisson assumption comes in? It looks to me
as if y ~ Gaussian, being generated by rmvnorm(). Also, just looking at y, it certainly doesn't look Poisson to me (non-integer values for one thing). Am I missing something?

If it's not an imposition, as a possibly related question: consider the model

   y = a + b*x + c*y + e

I think I understand how to estimate b and c when they're independent Gaussian. Can one do this for the case where they're bivariate normal with parametrized covariance (or precision) matrix?  (I was looking for an answer to this when I began to read up on the iid_n family).

Thanks!

messages.subject: spatial-temporal SPDE question
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a theoretical question and coding question.

I am fitting a spatial-temporal Poisson GLM using SPDE. I am following the space-time examples in Section 10.1 of the spde tutorial. And also the Godin et al paper.

The model that I consider is of the form:

Y_tj ~ Poisson(mu_tj)
log(mu_tj) = Covariates_tj * betas + v_tj
v_tj = rho * v_t-1,j  + u_tj

t is the time index. j is the observation within a year index.
Suppose we have 10 years of data...so t = 1, ..., 10.
And suppose we have 30 - 50 sampling locations per year. Sampling locations differ per year.

I have fitted this spatial-temporal model in INLA. That was easy (using the group argument).

Internally, INLA models the spatial correlated random effects u_tj as A * w. I understand that the projector matrix A consists in fact of 10 smaller projector matrices...and I am able to obtain and plot the 10 spatial random fields (1 picture per year). This is like Figure 6 in Godin et al.

I am also able to obtain the u_tj values ...and I can plot these for each year (e.g. by plotting spatial coordinates and use the u_tj value  as the size of the dot).

But how do I calculate the v_tj s? The code below does not work because the sampled locations differs per year:

v <- list()
v[[1]] <- u[1:SampleSize]
for (t in 2:10){
    I  <-   GroupIndex == t
    v[[t]] <- rho * v[[t-1]] + u[I]
}

And where would I get the year 1 values from?

Question 1: The simulation study in the spde tutorial (section 10.1) works the other way around. It simulates the v_tj s for each node of the mesh (so that Figure 10.1 in the spde tutorial can be made). And then the tutorial takes a subset. But when I fit the model, I can't get the  v_tj s. How do I get them so that I can see how they change over time?

Or in normal words....how can I calculate/obtain the temporal residuals from the AR1 part of the model.

Question 2: Why do people plot the spatial random fields (from a spatial-temporal AR1 model) that are used to calculate the u_tj s? Or formulated differently, why would you plot them for each year and compare them? See for example Figure 6 in Godin et al. These random fields are supposed to be independent over time. Is the interest not on the v_tj values?

Or in normal words: Why do people only focus on the pure-spatial component in the AR1 part of the model?

I can see that if every sampling location would be sampled in each year, then it would be easy to calculate both type of residuals (temporal and pure spatial).

Kind regards,
Pieter

So you have an f(..., model=spde, group=list(...,...="ar1")) model?

>
> Internally, INLA models the spatial correlated random effects u_tj as A * w.

This is the point where I'm not sure what you mean. The standard group construction above doesn't have the u:s explicitly anywhere, only the spatio-temporal field v itself.

>
> But how do I calculate the v_tj s? The code below does not work because the sampled locations differs per year:

Either an inla.mesh.project() call applied to the specific subsequence that corresponds to a specific year, or by multiplying the whole thing by an A matrix from

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=yourlocations, group=youryear, n.group=...)

How to extract the full vector of v-values depends on how you've defined the model. Easiest is if you've included a prediction stack, with e.g. tag="pred":
v <- inla.stack.index(stack, tag="pred")$data

Then
  my.v <- A % v
calculates the field values at yourlocations for youryear.

I'm not sure why I didn't include "group" and "replicate" in the inla.mesh.projector() interface when I wrote it; A clear oversight, and another item to put on my TODO list...

See above. Since I can't look at the Godin paper right now I have a hard time imagining how they do anything differently to this.

>
> Or in normal words....how can I calculate/obtain the temporal residuals from the AR1 part of the model.

Hmmm, the u:s are the temporal residuals, not the v:s. To get the u:s, you you could construct the A-matrix for each year, and then do something like
u2 <-  A2 %*% v - beta * A1 %*% v

>
> Question 2: Why do people plot the spatial random fields (from a spatial-temporal AR1 model) that are used to calculate the u_tj s? Or formulated differently, why would you plot them for each year and compare them? See for example Figure 6 in Godin et al. These random fields are supposed to be independent over time. Is the interest not on the v_tj values?

As above, usually the focus is on the v:s yes.  The u:s are the ones that would essentially be independent over time, correct.
Again, I don't know what they did in the paper, butone possible reason for looking at the u:s is to check that they do indeed appear to act as independent field, since if they don't that indicates something missing in the model.

> I can see that if every sampling location would be sampled in each year, then it would be easy to calculate both type of residuals (temporal and pure spatial).

In the Bayesian setting, all of these values always exist, we are just more or less confident about their true values...

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I would like to fit an ANOVA model with heteroscedasticity. How can I do it with INLA? I tried with a model="iid" for each treatment level, but the results look very strange.
See a small, reproducible example below.
(In the end, I would like to add other "random effects", but first I would like to understand this "simpler" case.)
Thanks in advance,
Tim

## model:
## goal: apply a treatment with B levels, and compare their means, while allowing for different error variances
## B: number of treatment levels
## N.b: number of subjects (one per treatment level)
## y_sb = mu + beta_b + e_sb with e_sb ~ N(0, sigma_b^2)

## simul
set.seed(1859)
B <- 3
N.b <- 50
N <- B * N.b
ids <- sprintf(fmt="id%03i", 1:N.b) # identifiers of the subjects
dat <- data.frame(block=rep(LETTERS[1:B], each=N.b),
                  id=rep(ids, B))
X <- model.matrix(~ 1 + block, data=dat)
mu <- 50
(beta <- c(mu, rnorm(n=B-1, mean=0, sd=3)))
(sigma.b <- setNames(sample(1:8, size=B, replace=ifelse(8 < B, TRUE, FALSE)),
                     levels(dat$block)))
epsilon <- do.call(c, lapply(sigma.b, function(sd.b){
  rnorm(n=N.b, mean=0, sd=sd.b)
}))
dat$y <- X %*% beta + epsilon
str(dat)
do.call(rbind, tapply(dat$y, dat$block, function(x){
  c("mean"=mean(x), "sd"=sd(x))
}))
boxplot(y ~ block, data=dat, varwidth=T, notch=T) # we can clearly see the different error variances

## fit via OLS
fit.ols <- lm(formula=y ~ 1 + block, data=dat)
summary(fit.ols)
dat2 <- cbind(dat,
              e.hat.ols=residuals(fit.ols))
dat2$e.hat.std.ols <- dat2$e.hat.ols / summary(fit.ols)$sigma
do.call(rbind, tapply(dat2$e.hat.std.ols, dat2$block, function(x){
  c("mean"=mean(x), "sd"=sd(x))
}))
boxplot(e.hat.std.ols ~ block, data=dat2, varwidth=T, notch=T) # assumption of homoscedasticity clearly violated

## fit via GLS
library(nlme)
fit.gls <- gls(model=y ~ 1 + block, data=dat,
               weights=varIdent(form=~1|block))
summary(fit.gls)
dat2 <- cbind(dat,
              e.hat.gls=residuals(fit.gls))
sigma.b.hat <- c(1, exp(coef(fit.gls$modelStruct$varStruct))) * fit.gls$sigma
dat2$e.hat.std.gls <- dat2$e.hat.gls / rep(sigma.b.hat, each=N.b)
do.call(rbind, tapply(dat2$e.hat.std.gls, dat2$block, function(x){
  c("mean"=mean(x), "sd"=sd(x))
}))
boxplot(e.hat.std.gls ~ block, data=dat2, varwidth=T, notch=T) # looks fine

## fit via INLA ?
library(INLA)
dat2 <- cbind(dat, model.matrix(~-1+dat$block))
colnames(dat2) <- c(colnames(dat), c("blockA", "blockB", "blockC"))
fit.inla <- inla(formula=y ~ 1 + f(blockA, model="iid") +
                   f(blockB, model="iid") +
                   f(blockC, model="iid"),
                 data=dat2)
summary(fit.inla) # results look very strange...

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tim,

there are three issues in your call to inla:

1. The model you are fitting in inla has 4 variance components: one for each block and the residual variance which is always there by default, and is provoking some confounding. You can fix it to a high precision using control.family().

2. You are not estimating group-level means. The iid models are centered at 0 by default. You could either remove this constraint or add the group means as fixed effects

3. When you use blockA/B/C variables for (f, iid) it is assuming that they are random effects with only two levels each (0 and 1). And trying to estimate a variance from there! What I think you wanted to do is to use id as a random effect weighted by blockA/B/C.

In summary, I believe this works as you expected:

dat2 <- transform(dat2, id2 = id, id3 = id)
fit.inla <- inla(formula=y ~ 0 + block + f(id, blockA, model="iid") +
                   f(id2, blockB, model="iid") +
                   f(id3, blockC, model="iid"),
                 control.family = list(
                   hyper = list(
                     prec = list(
                       initial = 10,
                       fixed = TRUE
                     )
                   )
                 ),
                 data=dat2)

summary(fit.inla)
1/sqrt(fit.inla$summary.hyperpar[,"mean"])

Best regards,

    ƒacu.-

A part of code as following:

z <- yp$count>0 +0

messages.subject_clean: Role of epsilon component in linear predictor
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a hierarchical model and am trying to draw replications of my dataset from the posterior predictive distribution. After some experimentation, I have managed to get myself rather confused about what I suspect is a simple matter. I hope that someone can easily set me straight. For the record, I'm aware that I can do an "NA replicate" trick to get posterior predictive draws as in this thread <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/r-inla-discussion-group/2FYu8lAqid4/fMpWiFcAE7AJ>, but I'm sufficiently disturbed by my lack of clarity here that I have the basics right first, rather than just blindly applying recipes! :)

Based on the Intro PDF <https://www.math.ntnu.no/~hrue/r-inla.org/doc/Intro/Intro.pdf>, I understand that the linear predictor eta_i is composed of my model terms as well as an iid epsilon_i  ~ N(0, lambda_eta). Then in addition to this, there is the "family noise", in my case student-T with unknown df and scale. I have an identity link.

If this is the case, then (based on the student-t likelihood documentation <http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/doc/likelihood/student-t.pdf>) I would expect that I should be able to do the following to draw from the posterior predictive. First obtain S posterior draws using inla.posterior.sample, and then for each draw s in 1, ..., S take the predicted values of eta_i from draw$latent -- call this vector eta_s -- and then one joint posterior predictive draw should be eta_s + rt(N, df=draw$hyperparam['df for t'])/sqrt(draw$hyperparam['precision for t'])

The problem is that, when I do this, the groups in the simulated replicates are all way more dispersed than they should be. This happens even with an intercept-only model, so it is not a matter of overfitting. It also happens if I use a plain Gaussian likelihood and eta_s + rnorm(N, sd=sqrt(1/draw$hyperparam['gaussian precision'])). Too much noise is being added.

Strangely, if I just take eta_s without adding the observation noise term, then I get summary statistics which behave roughly as I would expect. Which got me wondering about the epsilon_eta term -- is this actually where the likelihood comes in? It seems doubtful since the intro pretty clearly says without qualification that this is Gaussian and separate from the likelihood pi. However, it is strange to me that the model summary output says nothing about the estimated precision lambda_eta -- only the likelihood-related parameters. But of course everything seems strange when you don't understand it ;)

Would someone be so kind as to put me back on the right path? What is the role of these epsilon_i, and how are they distinct from the observation noise under identity link and Gaussian/t likelihood? Maybe in this special "degenerate" case, I need to use a hack like in the linked thread (setting the family to a fixed, high precision) to prevent overspecification? But then I'm limited to Gaussian (and not T)?

Many thanks,
Jonathan

messages.body_plain:
Do I understand you correct in that your
y = epsilon1 + epsilon 2 + more
Where epsilon1 is the likelihood (gaussian or student t), and epsilon2 is in the linear predictor?

This model does not really make sense, as you cannot separate the two independent noise contributions. I would expect this to lead to inflated variances. The model does not know which component to use, and so, in fitting it is using either, and in  prediction, it is using them both.

I do not think INLA works on this model, but as the model does not make sense, it is not considered a problem.
(If you fix the hyper-parameters in epsilon2, INLA should be able to fit the model. But this does not make the model sensible.)

Does that help?
Haakon

messages.subject_clean: Animal abundance model from replicate counts to estimate detection probability
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA folks,

I imagine this question has been asked before, but I have searched and can't find an answer. So here goes.

Wildlife biologists commonly use so-called 'N-Mixture' models to estimate animal abundance.  Sampling involves going to multiple sites in a study area, visiting each site, say, three times in short succession.   The purpose of the replicate counts per site is to quantify detection probability, so that this probability can be used to correct abundance estimates for imperfect detection. Estimates are otherwise biased low, and using zero-inflated models doesn't always help.  Both counts and detection probability are often modeled with covariates.  These models are often evaluated using BUGS and they look like this:

    # Ecological model for true abundance
    for (i in 1:R){
      N[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
      log(lambda[i]) <- alpha0 + alpha1 * X[i]
      # Observation model for replicated counts
      for (j in 1:T){
        y[i,j] ~ dbin(p[i,j], N[i])
        p[i,j] <- exp(lp[i,j])/(1+exp(lp[i,j]))
        lp[i,j] <- beta0 + beta1 * X[i]
      } #j
    } #i

Is there a way to evaluate this type of model using INLA?  I suspect there might be, using 'copy' or 'replicate', or specifying multiple distributions like 'c(binomial, poisson)', but I am not clever enough to figure this out. If this could be done in INLA, it would make model evaluation A LOT quicker and allow convenient ways to code spatiotemporal random effects.

I have attached code to simulate data and analyze it using OpenBugs, in case that is helpful.

Thanks,
Tim

Hi,

the paralellisation strategy used in the code, like when and what to
paralellise and the (max) number of threads used, depends on the size
of the  model. this is just empirical, as trying to optimize the speed,
like if the model is small, paralellisation just slow things down and
its runs faster in serial mode.

giving num.threads=N, only gives maximum number of threads that can be
used, but if the empirical found strategy (as above) suggest fewer,
then fewer is used.

the only option to 'force' more threads to be used, is to override the
size of the problem, by saying

control.compute = list(openmp.strategy = "huge")

which turn on everything. see ?control.compute for more options. In any
case, the run-time system will determine how many threads that are used
in the end.

the RAM:  what is important is the RAM per thread, so if the machine
has X Gb RAM and you run with N threads, then X/N is the key number. If
this is to low, then you need to increase X (not easy) or decrease N
(easy).

Also strategy="gaussian" will helps (as done in the code below), as it
reduce internal storage.

Best,
H

# Scale coordinates
coord.scale <- 1e-6
data$xs <- data$x * coord.scale
data$ys <- data$y * coord.scale
coord <- cbind(data$xs, data$ys)

# Create mesh
boundary1 <- inla.nonconvex.hull(points = coord, convex = 0.05)
boundary2 <- inla.nonconvex.hull(points = coord, convex = 0.50)
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc = coord, boundary = list(boundary1, boundary2), cutoff = 2e4 * coord.scale,
                     max.edge = c(5e4, 6e5) * coord.scale, offset  = c(1e4, 1e6) * coord.scale)

# Set spatial prior
mesh.width <- min(diff(range(mesh$loc[,1])), diff(range(mesh$loc[,2])))
spde <- local.inla.spde2.matern.new <http://local.inla.spde2.matern.new>(mesh = mesh, prior.pc.rho = c(mesh.width / 2, 0.5), prior.pc.sig = c(1, 0.5))

# Get temporal and spatial indexes
year <- data$year
year.index <- year - min(year) + 1
n.year <- length(unique(year.index))
spatial.index <- inla.spde.make.index("spatial", n.spde = spde$n.spde, n.group = n.year)

# Create observation stack
A.obs <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = coord, group = year.index, n.group = n.year)
covariates.obs <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x4", "x6", "x7", "x8")
effects.obs <- list(c(spatial.index, list(intercept = 1)), list(data[, covariates.obs]))
stack.obs <- inla.stack(data = list(count = data$count, E = data$effort), A = list(A.obs, 1), effects = effects.obs, tag = "obs")

# Create prediction stack
coord.mesh <- cbind(rep(mesh$loc[,1], n.year), rep(mesh$loc[,2], n.year))
A.pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = coord.mesh, group = rep(1:n.year, each = mesh$n), n.group = n.year)
effects.pred <- list(c(spatial.index, list(intercept = 1)))
stack.pred <- inla.stack(data = list(count = NA, E = 1), A = list(A.pred), effects = effects.pred, tag = "pred")

# Combine stacks
stack.all <- inla.stack(stack.obs, stack.pred)
data.stack <- inla.stack.data(stack = stack.all, spde = spde)

# Specify model formula
formula <- count ~ -1 + intercept + x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 + x6 + x7 + x8 +
  f(spatial, model = spde, group = spatial.group, control.group = list(model = "ar1"))

# Estimate model
result <- inla(formula, data = data.stack, family = "nbinomial", E = data$E,
               control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack.all), link = 1, compute = TRUE),
               control.compute = list(cpo = TRUE, dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE, mlik = TRUE),
               verbose = TRUE)

Thanks to Rue or others who might be able to help.

James
